top_news.title: Open Source AI Gap Map
top_news.dek: Current AI has launched a 'Gap Map' indexing 421 open-source AI products across 14 categories.
top_news.brief: The project, backed by $400 million in funding, categorizes 266 tools, 85 models, 50 datasets, and 20 hardware projects. It aims to provide a comprehensive view of the open-source AI stack to identify development gaps and support public-option AI infrastructure.
top_news.image_alt: Visualization of the open-source AI ecosystem stack

top_news.title: A 26,000-student study shows AI's hidden learning cost takes two full years to surface
top_news.dek: A longitudinal study of 26,000 students reveals that AI-assisted homework leads to a 24% decline in exam performance over two years.
top_news.brief: Researchers found that while AI tools like DeepSeek and Qwen help students complete assignments faster and achieve higher grades initially, the long-term impact is a significant degradation in core competency. The study suggests that short-term metrics fail to capture the cognitive atrophy caused by over-reliance on LLMs for academic tasks.
top_news.image_alt: Chart showing the divergence between homework grades and exam performance over a two-year period.

top_news.title: Agentic coding notes from Galapagos Island
top_news.dek: Practical reflections on agentic coding highlight the paradox of scaling AI workflows despite frequent, high-risk errors.
top_news.brief: The author notes that AI agents often produce work that would be grounds for termination if performed by a human. Despite this, the efficiency gains encourage developers to scale these agents further. The piece emphasizes the difficulty of debugging complex UI issues and the limitations of current LLM-based bisecting strategies in codebases lacking robust test suites.
top_news.image_alt: Conceptual diagram of an agentic coding loop with human oversight.

primary.title: UK's AI Security Institute finds standard benchmarks systematically underestimate what AI agents can actually do
primary.summary: In a study covering seven benchmarks, the UK's AI Security Institute shows that standard AI evaluations systematically underestimate agent capabilities by capping the compute budget. On software engineering tasks, success rates jumped about 25 percent when the token budget was increased tenfold. Newer models benefit the most. Depending on the token budget, actual progress at the frontier is about 60 percent steeper than previous measurements suggested, according to AISI. The article UK's AI Security Institute finds standard benchmarks systematically underestimate what AI agents can actually do
